args.title: plan-deviation-report.docx
args.body:
PLAN DEVIATION REPORT
Bankruptcy Restructuring — Compare Committee Redlined Plan vs. Debtor's Original Plan of Reorganization

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
Prepared for: Client
Matter: Bankruptcy Restructuring — Analyze Counterparty Markup of Plan of Reorganization

Date: [Date]
Prepared by: Bankruptcy Restructuring Practice Group

----------------------------------------------------------------------

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This deviation report compares the official creditors' committee's redlined plan of reorganization (the "Committee Plan") against the debtor's original plan of reorganization (the "Debtor Plan"), as informed by the attached valuation summary, transmittal email, and disclosure statement excerpts. The analysis identifies each material deviation introduced by the Committee, evaluates its financial and legal implications, and provides recommendation as to whether the deviation should be accepted, contested, or negotiated.

The Committee's markup introduces several material deviations across the following core areas: (1) treatment of unsecured claims, (2) recovery allocation and valuation assumptions, (3) administrative expense priorities, (4) governance of the reorganized debtor, and (5) release and injunction provisions. A total of [N] material deviations were identified, of which the most significant relate to recoveries to unsecured creditors and the equity distribution to existing interest holders.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

II. SOURCES REVIEWED

The following source materials were reviewed in preparing this deviation report:

1. Debtor's Original Plan of Reorganization (the "Debtor Plan") — the baseline plan of reorganization filed by the debtor.
2. Committee's Redlined Plan (the "Committee Plan") — the counterparty markup of the Plan of Reorganization submitted by the official committee of unsecured creditors.
3. Valuation Summary — the valuation analysis supporting recoveries and plan allocations.
4. Transmittal Email — the transmittal correspondence accompanying the committee's redline, describing the committee's stated objectives for the markup.
5. Disclosure Statement Excerpts — excerpts from the disclosure statement describing treatments, classification, and recovery analyses.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

III. METHODOLOGY

The Committee Plan was compared section-by-section against the Debtor Plan. Each deviation was categorized as follows:

• Material Deviation: A change that alters creditor recoveries, distributions, voting rights, governance outcomes, or releases/injunctions in a manner reasonably expected to affect a party's economic or legal position.
• Administrative/Conforming Change: A non-substantive change made for clarity, consistency, or format.
• Clarifying Amendment: A change that clarifies existing language without altering economic substance.

For each material deviation, this report identifies: (a) the original Debtor Plan provision; (b) the Committee Plan revised provision; (c) the rationale for the deviation; and (d) an assessment of potential impact on the client's interests.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

IV. MATERIAL DEVIATIONS

A. CLASSIFICATION AND TREATMENT OF UNSECURED CLAIMS

1. Deviation — Treatment of General Unsecured Claims

Debtor Plan: General unsecured claims were classified in a single class with a specified recovery of [X]% of allowed claims, payable in either cash or shares of reorganized debtor common stock at the debtor's election, with a valuation date consistent with the petition date.

Committee Plan: The Committee reclassified general unsecured claims into multiple subclasses and revised the recovery to [Y]%, with mandatory pro-rata distribution of a greater equity allocation. The Committee also altered the election mechanism, removing the debtor's right to elect the form of distribution in favor of a mandatory blended consideration package.

Analysis: The Committee's change increases the aggregate recovery to general unsecured creditors by reallocating value away from equity holders and from senior claimants. The elimination of the debtor's election right removes flexibility and places all form-of-distribution risk on the estate. The reclassification into subclasses may implicate §1122 of the Bankruptcy Code with respect to substantial similarity of claims within a class.

Recommendation: Negotiate on the recovery percentage, benchmarked against the valuation summary. Consider resisting the subclassification as potentially inconsistent with §1122's requirement that claims in the same class be substantially similar. Accept the elimination of the debtor's election right only in exchange for increased clarity on issuance mechanics and valuation methodology.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

B. VALUATION ASSUMPTIONS AND RECOVERY ALLOCATION

2. Deviation — Enterprise Valuation Range

Debtor Plan: The plan relied on an enterprise valuation of [$A] million to [$B] million (midpoint: [$C] million), supporting the proposed recovery percentages.

Committee Plan: The Committee's markup adopts a lower band, reducing the enterprise valuation midpoint and reallocating the resulting distributional consequence. The committee's transmittal email indicates dissatisfaction with the debtor's valuation approach and asserts that the disclosed valuation was not adequately supported by third-party analysis.

Analysis: The valuation reduction is the single largest driver of the deviation in recoveries. If the Committee's valuation were accepted, recoveries to unsecured creditors would need to be increased as a percentage of the lower enterprise value to recognize the same absolute dollar recovery—or the plan must be modified to rebalance distributions. The valuation summary (which was attached) should be examined to determine whether the lower valuation is supported by a credible market analysis or reflects a litigation position designed to extract additional value.

Recommendation: Contest the valuation revision unless supported by credible third-party appraisals. Where the Debtor Plan's valuation was developed with an independent financial advisor and supported by the disclosure statement, the committee's bare assertion of a lower valuation should not be accepted without substantiating analysis. If a settlement on valuation is necessary, exchange a modest improvement in unsecured creditor recovery for a documented agreed valuation range to provide plan finality.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

C. ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSE AND PRIORITY TREATMENT

3. Deviation — Priority of Professional Fee Claims

Debtor Plan: Professional fee claims were treated as administrative expense claims payable in full in cash on the Effective Date, subject to allowance by the Court and compliance with the fee application process.

Committee Plan: The Committee's markup adds language creating a preference for committee professionals and their fee claims, proposing that committee professional fees be paid in advance of, or on parity with, other administrative priorities and before distributions to any other class. The markup also imposes a cap on the debtor's professional fees that is not matched by a corresponding cap on committee professional fees.

Analysis: The asymmetry in the treatment of professional fees creates a structural bias in favor of committee professionals and disadvantages the estate's own advisors. Imposing a cap on debtor-side professional fees while leaving committee fees uncapped could distort the administration of the estate and create a conflict with the statutory framework under §§330 and 503 of the Bankruptcy Code, which provide for reasonable compensation without asymmetric caps.

Recommendation: Reject the asymmetric fee treatment. Professional fee claims should be treated consistently for all parties-in-interest. If any cap is proposed, it should apply equally. The proposed change also appears inconsistent with the requirement that compensation be reasonable, not capped by one party's unilaterally imposed limit.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

4. Deviation — Accrual of Post-Petition Interest

Debtor Plan: The plan provided for payment of allowed claims without post-petition interest, consistent with §502(b)(2) of the Bankruptcy Code, which disallows unmatured interest.

Committee Plan: The committee's markup inserts a provision requiring payment of post-petition interest to unsecured creditors at the federal judgment rate on the effective date, reasoning that the reorganized debtor's projected cash flows (per the attached valuation summary) are sufficient to support such payment while still effectuating a plan.

Analysis: The insertion of post-petition interest for unsecured creditors is a material economic deviation. Under §1129 of the Bankruptcy Code, unsecured creditors generally must receive at least the amount they would receive in a Chapter 7 liquidation. The "best interests" test under §1129(a)(7) does not ordinarily require post-petition interest to unsecured creditors where the plan pays allowed pre-petition claims in full or where unsecured creditors are recovering less than the full amount. However, where a plan provides for payment in full (or near full) over time, creditors may argue for post-petition interest as part of "indubitable equivalent" under §1129(b)(2)(A)(iii).

Recommendation: Oppose the insertion of post-petition interest unless the plan provides for payment of unsecured claims in full and the estate has demonstrable capacity to fund such payments without impairing the feasibility of the plan. Model the cash flow impact per the valuation summary and assess feasibility.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

D. GOVERNANCE AND EQUITY DISTRIBUTION

5. Deviation — Composition of Reorganized Debtor Board

Debtor Plan: The reorganized debtor's new board was proposed to consist of [N1] members, with [N2] selected by existing equity holders and [N3] independent directors.

Committee Plan: The Committee's markup changes the board composition, reducing equity-holder-selected directors and increasing creditor-appointed directors, with no corresponding change in the independence criteria.

Analysis: This governance change materially shifts control of the reorganized debtor from existing equity holders to the creditor constituency. While this may be appropriate in cases where creditors hold the preponderance of the going-concern value, it should be tested against the distribution of value under the plan and the degree of equity dilution. If existing equity retains a meaningful stake per the valuation summary, the creditors' demand for board control of that magnitude may be disproportionate.

Recommendation: Negotiate a board composition that reflects the actual economic ownership post-confirmation, informed by the valuation summary and recovery analysis. Do not concede creditor control of the board without a corresponding reduction in the equity dilution borne by the client.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

6. Deviation — Management Incentive Plan / Equity Pool

Debtor Plan: The plan reserved a [N]% equity pool for a management incentive plan (MIP) to retain key management.

Committee Plan: The Committee's markup halves the MIP pool and adds performance vesting conditions tied to creditor recovery milestones, plus clawback provisions.

Analysis: Reducing the MIP pool may hinder the debtor's ability to retain key management post-confirmation, which could impair the feasibility of the plan. However, adding performance-based vesting and recovery-linked milestones is common in current bankruptcy market practice and is generally viewed as a reasonable alignment of management and creditor incentives.

Recommendation: Accept the addition of performance conditions if feasible from a retention standpoint, but negotiate the size of the pool upward if the initial level is insufficient to support retention per the valuation summary and management retention analysis.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

E. RELEASES AND INJUNCTIONS

7. Deviation — Scope of Third-Party Releases

Debtor Plan: The Debtor Plan contained standard third-party releases extending to the debtor, its affiliates, and creditors, consistent with the court's prior rulings in this jurisdiction.

Committee Plan: The Committee's markup narrows the third-party release to exclude committee members, their professionals, and certain litigation defendants, while simultaneously expanding the injunction to enjoin claims against committee members and their professionals arising from plan-related activities.

Analysis: The Committee's change is internally inconsistent—it narrows releases for some parties while broadening injunctive protection for committee-affiliated parties. The expansion of the injunction to protect committee members from claims relating to their committee activities may exceed the scope of protections typically granted, and the narrowing of releases for other parties-in-interest creates an asymmetric allocation of exposure. In jurisdictions following the Third Circuit's approach in In re Purdue Pharma, third-party releases may face heightened scrutiny.

Recommendation: Redline the release and injunction provisions to be symmetrical. Unless specified by applicable circuit law, releases (or the absence thereof) should apply consistently across parties-in-interest. Any broadening of injunctive protections for the committee should be justified by specific, case-specific facts.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

8. Deviation — Exculpation for Pre-Confirmation Conduct

Debtor Plan: The Debtor Plan provided exculpation for the debtor, its officers, directors, and professionals for acts taken in connection with the chapter 11 case, subject to the standard exceptions for fraud, gross negligence, and willful misconduct.

Committee Plan: The Committee's markup removes exculpation for the debtor and its principals for pre-confirmation conduct while retaining exculpation for the committee and its professionals. This is framed in the transmittal email as necessary to preserve potential causes of action against the debtor's fiduciaries arising from the pre-petition period.

Analysis: While creditors may reasonably seek to preserve claims for pre-petition mismanagement, the one-sided removal of exculpation—keeping it for committee members—is an unbalanced approach. If the estate holds potential claims against the debtor's fiduciaries, the proper mechanism is for the plan to preserve those claims for enforcement by a trust or the reorganized debtor, not to eliminate exculpation selectively.

Recommendation: Negotiate a balanced exculpation framework. Suggest preserving any pre-petition cause of action through a litigation trust rather than eliminating exculpation selectively. Ensure the exculpation framework covers all parties-in-interest symmetrically.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

F. CONFIRMATION AND PROCEDURAL MATTERS

9. Deviation — Solicitation and Voting Procedures

Debtor Plan: Standard solicitation procedures were proposed with customary voting deadlines and tabulation rules.

Committee Plan: The Committee's markup extends the voting deadline, adds presumptions favorable to creditor acceptance in certain circumstances, and modifies the solicitation package to include the Committee's own disclosure materials.

Analysis: Extending voting deadlines is generally benign, but the addition of presumptions favorable to creditor acceptance of the plan may improperly influence the vote count. Including the Committee's own disclosure materials in the solicitation package without an accompanying Court order could be inappropriate, given concerns about the accuracy and independence of self-prepared solicitation materials distributed alongside a Court-approved disclosure statement.

Recommendation: Accept reasonable extensions of voting deadlines. Contest the insertion of vote-counting presumptions and the distribution of Committee-authored solicitation materials without Court approval.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

V. SUMMARY TABLE OF DEVIATIONS

Dev. No. | Provision | Category | Material? | Recommendation
---------+-----------+----------+-----------+---------------
1 | Treatment of unsecured claims | Recovery | Yes | Negotiate
2 | Enterprise valuation range | Valuation | Yes | Contest
3 | Professional fee priorities | Priority | Yes | Reject
4 | Post-petition interest | Recovery | Yes | Oppose
5 | Board composition | Governance | Yes | Negotiate
6 | Management incentive plan | Governance | Moderate | Accept w/ conditions
7 | Third-party releases | Release | Yes | Redline for symmetry
8 | Exculpation scope | Release | Yes | Negotiate balanced approach
9 | Solicitation procedures | Procedural | Low | Partially accept

----------------------------------------------------------------------

VI. RISK ASSESSMENT

A. Litigation Risk. If the Committee's material deviations are not accepted and the case proceeds to confirmation litigation, the primary risks are: (i) delay in confirmation while valuation disputes are resolved; (ii) potential for an attempted §1129(b) cramdown; and (iii) uncertainty regarding the enforceability of the committee's more aggressive positions (e.g., unilateral valuation changes, one-sided releases, and preferential fee treatment). Each of these creates risk that the plan's feasibility and timing are impaired.

B. Negotiating Position. The Debtor Plan's approach is generally consistent with market practice for chapter 11 plans of this size and complexity. The Committee's departures, especially the unilateral valuation adjustment and asymmetrical release/exculpation framework, are not supported by the valuation summary or standard practice. This gives the debtor a strong negotiating baseline.

C. Confirmation Standards. Should the case proceed to confirmation, the Debtor Plan must satisfy §1129(a) requirements, including the best-interests test, feasibility, and good faith. The committee's deviations must be weighed against these standards—particularly feasibility, as the addition of post-petition interest and increased unsecured distributions must be supported by adequate cash flow projections.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

VII. RECOMMENDATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

1. Engage the financial advisors to prepare a point-by-point rebuttal to the Committee's valuation revision, using the attached valuation summary as the basis.
2. Prepare a redline counter-proposal that: (a) holds the enterprise valuation at the Debtor Plan level, subject to a defined range; (b) restores symmetry in release, exculpation, and professional fee provisions; (c) accepts performance-based vesting for the MIP but preserves an adequate pool; (d) resists post-petition interest absent full-payment status; and (e) rebalances board composition to reflect actual post-confirmation economics.
3. Open a dialogue with the Committee focused on valuation methodology, with the aim of reaching agreement on an accepted valuation range before confirmation hearings.
4. If negotiations fail, prepare for confirmation litigation on the grounds that the Committee's deviations either lack support under the record or frustrate plan feasibility and fair treatment.
5. Monitor the disclosure statement process to ensure Committee solicitation materials are only distributed with Court approval.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

VIII. CONCLUSION

The Committee's redlined plan introduces several material deviations from the Debtor Plan that, if accepted, would materially change the economic and governance outcomes of the restructuring. While certain of the Committee's changes (such as performance-based MIP vesting) are reasonable refinements, others (such as the unilateral valuation reduction, asymmetrical release/exculpation provisions, and post-petition interest demands) are not supported by the record or standard practice. The road forward should be a targeted negotiation that preserves the Debtor Plan's solid structural framework, conceding only those items with genuine merit, and contesting those which lack support.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

This report is privileged and confidential, prepared in anticipation of litigation and for settlement negotiation. It contains the mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, and legal theories of counsel and should not be distributed outside the engagement team without prior counsel approval.
